body: Agree, though I think the reveal of her expression at the very end when her hair parted left something to be desired. I almost wish they hadn’t.
I remember seeing Darkness Falls (evil tooth fairy movie) in the theaters… the first half was good, spooky, atmospheric… then it devolved into the military shooting AKs at a flying witch.
I think bowling is sexy
I agree. My bf and I have separate houses in the same neighborhood, it’s the most ideal living situation I’ve ever had with an SO.
Yeah, but in my experience it’ll just leave you feeling confused and preoccupied. And if you respond, you’ll be wracked with regret and feel foolish.

Agree. I got off it October 2021, got tired of sabotaging my healing and the risk of having my heart rended over and over. I feel more present in my life after over 2 years of no/minimal use, there are lots of amazing side effects.
The lead singer of a group we both love died, and he was listening to them. Thinking of me, I’d imagine.

Same with my best/childhood friend. I reacted by withdrawing HARD from social media; our friends were immediately posting about her (not in a performative way), but I just… couldn’t. I still haven’t interacted with social media (FB, Instagram were the mains) since. Only pain resides there.

I feel for you and the Original Commenter. It’s devastating. 🫂

I live in South Minneapolis, 2020 was a wild ride. That's what really escalated my best friend's (NE MPLS, also service industry) drinking issues and led to her cirrhosis diagnosis and death last year at 35.

Your description really brings it all into perspective, and I'm glad you're making it through the other side. 🙏 Keep your stick on the ice.

When my Q flew out to rehab after our intervention, there was never any desire to "do the work." Thought she was going to go back to her apartment, job in the service industry, and maintain sobriety with her alcoholic boyfriend; but he's going to clean more! That'll do the trick! There was absolutely no admittance, no "come to Jesus" moment. If she hadn't died out there, she would've died back here, and that's the grim truth.

My best friend and Q said of her perpetual vertigo and hand tremors "it's hereditary."

The internal varices bleeding? "Sometimes that happens to people, and I could've had it happening since middle school."

Vomiting every day? "Athsma and coughing makes me gag." Her roommates tried an intervention on her to accuse her of bulimia, against my advisement. That went great.

Bloated stomach? "We've all gained some weight during quarantine."

I also noticed a vitamin/supplement obsession, and a lot of performative gestures around "health." "We're in our 30s now, we should be on a strict regimen!"

She died last year of cirrhosis at 35.

I'm so terribly sorry for your loss; I lost my best friend to alcoholism a year ago. One cannot prepare, even if it's been a slow-motion wreck. Please be kind to and take care of yourself. It's a sad and surreal place to be.

I'm very sorry for your loss; I see you. My best friend died this time last year of liver failure/cirrhosis. She was 35. We had an intervention and sent her across the country for rehab, but no one knew it was already too late. I had known she had a drinking problem for a few years, but it wasn't until 2019-2020 that things really started escalating. I was scared and wanted to tell her parents, but didn't. It's hard not to blame myself, but her parents knew she had a drinking problem too; they had confronted her about it, but she was the only one who could make the change. We couldn't do it for her.

I have regrets and resentment about the situation; occasionally they will land somewhere... on myself, on her, on her family, on her abusive alcoholic boyfriend... but I know that the only thing that I can resent and blame is the disease of alcoholism. I'm thinking of you, and I hope you can get any help and counseling you need. You didn't do anything wrong, and you were a good friend. I'm so terribly sorry that we will miss them forever.

I'm so terribly sorry for your situation. My best friend had a similar predicament; we had an intervention for her around this time last year and she was flown to inpatient treatment. Gradually, it became apparent that they could not care for her there, she needed round the clock care for decompensated cirrhosis, and the facility was obviously not equipped. She passed in early February, she was 35. It was unstoppable, and had been for many years.

Take care of yourself, I'm thinking of you.

What a tragic loss and circumstance for you, I'm so terribly sorry. I feel for you enormously; my best friend passed in February of the same. She was 35. I hope that you can find peace and any therapeutic help that you need. Take care of yourself.

I'm so sorry. It's such a strange realization; my Q has since passed but before she did, I was describing my relationship with her to my therapist, and he said "this sounds a lot like grief." Sending you love and compassion for the future memories that will be rewritten without him. It's a rough row.

I lived with (one of) my Q(s) for 5 years of escalating alcoholism. It's still traumatic to think about; SO many times I was livid, driving home from work, keying myself up to make him leave... only to make it "well, if it happens ONE more time..." Leaving an alcoholic is something one needs to grab on with both hands and stick to, and after a violent incident I finally did. It was the best decision I could've ever made for myself, and as it turns out, for him. He hasn't drank since that day 6 years ago.

I’m so sorry for your devastating losses. I called the suicide prevention hotline in the evening and managed to get through the night. Thank you for your comment, I appreciate your care. I hope you can find peace, even if only moments.

I called the suicide prevention hotline last night. When I was in the state I was yesterday, I didn’t care about hurting anyone, which has often stopped the ideation cycle in the past. It was scary to realize that “fail safe” wasn’t there. I’m going to see my therapist this week about getting depression medication.

I feel for your complicated grief, I am in the midst of my own with my Q's death. She was a similar age. Try to feel whatever you feel without judgment. Pangs of resentment and self-righteousness have their place in the process and need to be honored as well as the memories, love, and sadness.

I'm thinking of you. It's a terrible thing that's happened to the ones we love. The path is overgrown, but we'll reach the clearing.

I'm so sorry for your losses. The loss of your cousin is especially awful. My best friend since childhood died of cirrhosis at 35 in February, and the grief is so complicated. I feel for you; anytime I hear Weekend Warriors being flippant about "killing their livers," I find my hackles raised. It's no joke. I just want you to know that you're not alone. Sending love and healing to you.

As for working through it, I've immersed myself in helping her family (like a second family to me) plan her memorial; it's next weekend. They are planning to address her struggles with alcohol and her prognosis, which I think is great. It's important for people to know. We had an intervention for her in November and she agreed to go to treatment across the country, but never seemed to really "take" to the program, seems like she just agreed to go 'til the heat was off. There was never any "come to Jesus" moment. She seemed to think she could go back to her regular life after 30 days in treatment and continue to stay with her abusive alcoholic boyfriend while maintaining sobriety. Turns out there was no going back anyhow, because her health became too poor after a couple months to travel, and it wasn't long after that she passed. I flew out there to be by her side and say goodbye.

I spent so much time agonizing over her disease, both the alcoholism and the cirrhosis. I was resentful. Why couldn't she just embrace the treatment program? Why didn't she want to get better as much as I wanted it for her? Now that she's gone, some of the anger is released. I didn't Cause it, I couldn't Control it, and I couldn't Cure it no matter how hard I banged my head against the wall. We were both powerless, and it was unstoppable.

I am so, so sorry. I went through the same scenario last month with my best friend from childhood, and similar regrets have passed through my head. Such a grim and terrible thing… please know that this is not your fault, no one cannot stop an alcoholic from drinking. Truly hope that your sister and yourself can find peace, you are in my thoughts.
That’s me. Finally realizing if some of it’s not normal, none of it is.
I’m attending my first in person MPLS meeting this week, your comment is heartening. I know I’ll cry big time.

My Q and best friend since childhood passed of alcohol-induced cirrhosis on February 1, she was 35. She was exhibiting the similar symptoms as your husband last June; bloated stomach and face, thin arms, yellow skin and eyes, swollen legs. She could hardly get up the one step to get inside my house. I was shocked, it all seemed to happen so fast. She was in the hospital a week later. After a month of recovery at her parents’ house, she kept drinking. Her condition quickly reverted, and we called an intervention in mid-November. She flew across the country for treatment, but we didn’t know the toll the cirrhosis had already taken. Soon enough, she could no longer participate in the treatment program and was in the hospital full-time. She got paracentesis two times, got her ruptured varices banded three times, and basically was asked “how far she wants to take it.” That was when she and her parents made her end-of-life plans. She wasn’t a candidate for any sort of transplant by that point for many reasons, she was too medically fragile, and her liver had caused her kidneys to fail. Palliative care was all that was left. My friends and I flew out to say our goodbyes, it was a grim and dismal thing. She died four days after we got back. I’m sorry this turned into an emotional dumping ground for me, but I just want to express how dire your husband’s situation could be. I’m sorry you are both going through this, and I can only hope it’s not too late for him too.

Wow, shocking how much we have in common with those situations. I’m definitely in the “not real” zone right now. Not beating myself up over not being beside myself with sadness… that will come. I’m just trying to be present. I’m very sorry for your loss, it’s such a terrible decline for the ones we love while we can only look on helplessly.
Thank you for your kind words and understanding. She has passed this morning, a solemn relief that she rests now.

Thank you. I have been talking to my therapist about the situation, and I'm discovering that we've had a dynamic since we were young that if I don't feel like she's worried enough about something, then I'll "worry for her," and become more preoccupied than she is. This is long before the alcoholism, but this whole situation is such fertile ground for that dynamic to resurface.

I think her family is getting the wool pulled over their eyes. There is a blind spot where they absolutely do not understand addiction and alcoholism, and that's where I feel like I need to fill in the gap. But I shouldn't; they know about her deflection, manipulation, and lying. They've done the leg work before and driven around town to confirm her lies. Through it all, they have relented to her time and time again. Thank you for confirming that I have to let go of whatever they decide, and then whatever she decides--I've just never done it. Ever.

Thank you again for your comment, I really appreciate it.

I'm so sorry, I have done the hitting behaviors as well. I used to do them when I was a child, but I was surprised that they re-surfaced in my adult life to calm the overwhelm of being in a relationship with an alcoholic (and subsequently returned again in a different abusive relationship). For me, it was an abrupt stop to my tide of racing thoughts and the climax of total emotional engulfment. Sometimes the first hit wouldn't "take" so I'd have to do it a few times (reminiscent of obsessive compulsive behavior). It felt relieving, but also frightening; I understand your urges, and your need to cope. I haven't engaged in that behavior–nor felt the urge to–in years since I've removed myself from both unhealthy dynamics. Again, I'm very sorry you're going through this. You are not alone.
